The Brown thornbill (Acanthiza uropygialis) is a small insectivorous passerine endemic to the arid and semi-arid woodlands of Australia. One of the most fundamental life-history parameters for this species is the mass of the newly hatched nestling. Upon emergence from the egg, following an incubation period that is sensitive to thermal conditions, a typical neonate weighs approximately 1.18 grams [Ww0 = approximately 1.18 grams]. This initial wet weight is remarkably consistent across broods and represents a modest starting point for the rapid growth that will occur during the nestling phase. The duration of the incubation period itself, however, is strongly influenced by ambient temperature. Field studies employing nest temperature loggers have demonstrated that, when the average nest temperature is maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], development proceeds at a predictable rate and hatching occurs after approximately 19 days [ab = approximately 19 days]. This developmental duration aligns well with values reported for other Acanthiza species of comparable size, underscoring the typical pace of embryogenesis in this lineage under moderate thermal regimes. The interplay between initial hatchling mass and the thermal environment during incubation is critical for subsequent chick survival.

As the nestling progresses through the brooding period, a crucial developmental milestone is the achievement of fledging, when the young bird first leaves the nest and begins to exercise its flight muscles. In the Brown thornbill, this transition from a nest-dependent chick to a fledgling is tightly linked to body temperature regulation. This relatively short nestling phase is typical of many small Australian passerines, which must develop quickly to escape high predation pressure. The ability to achieve flight at this early age is supported by a high metabolic capacity. Comparative respirometry trials conducted at this same body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] have measured a resting metabolic rate of 31.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 31.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the high energetic demands of thermoregulation and rapid tissue synthesis in a bird of this diminutive size.

Following fledging, the juvenile bird enters a period of rapid somatic growth and physiological maturation. The elevated basal oxygen consumption of 31.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 31.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour] established during the nestling phase continues to fuel the rapid tissue synthesis required for achieving adult dimensions at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. A key milestone in this post-fledging period is the attainment of sexual maturity. A detailed study of gonadal development in free-living individuals revealed that, under the warm conditions typical of the species' active foraging period (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), the time since birth at puberty is reached at 57 days [tp = 57 days]. This relatively early maturation is a common life-history strategy among small, short-lived passerines, allowing individuals to quickly enter the breeding population. The rapid developmental trajectory is mirrored in the final body size achieved. Adult females, which are the slightly smaller sex, reach an ultimate wet weight of 6.2 grams [Wwi = 6.2 grams], while adult males, showing a subtle degree of sexual dimorphism, attain a maximum adult body mass of 6.5 grams [Wwi = 6.5 grams]. This size difference is consistent with a minor sex-role differentiation observed during the breeding season.

Regarding the annual reproductive output, females typically lay a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. Each clutch contains between 2 and 4 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch contains between 2 and 4 eggs], a modest fecundity that reflects the high survival probability of the young in a relatively stable, albeit resource-limited, environment. The decision to produce only one brood annually is likely an adaptation to the harsh, seasonal climate of the arid interior.

The overall longevity of the Brown thornbill is ultimately constrained by the high energetic demands of its rapid early development. While the species exhibits a rapid developmental rate and a relatively early first reproduction, its overall lifespan is moderate for a small passerine. The oldest documented individuals in wild populations have been recorded to persist for as long as 4,198 days [am = 4,198 days] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This lifespan reflects the balance between the high metabolic costs of a small body and the potential for long-term survival in a predator-rich but resource-consistent ecosystem. This lifespan data, when integrated with the average annual fecundity, paints a picture of a species with a comparatively slower demography for its size, investing in the survival of a few well-provisioned offspring each year rather than a large clutch multiple times. The long-term ecological success of Acanthiza uropygialis across its broad range is a testament to the efficacy of this specific life-history combination.
